title: Quebec MNAs must swear oath to the King, judge rules
summary: A Quebec Superior Court judge has suspended the province’s law that made the mandatory oath to King Charles optional, ordering that members of the province's legislature must swear allegiance before…

image.caption: Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon speaks at the National Assembly during the swearing-in ceremony of Parti Québécois (PQ) MNAs in October. (Sylvain Roy Roussel/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Quebec Superior Court Justice Ian Demers will deliver his decision today on a lawyer's attempts to block the start of parliamentary work this week, after the province's MNAs unanimously renounced the Oath of Allegiance during last month's swearing-in ceremonies.
Lawyer claims members' refusal to take oath threatens National Assembly's legitimacy
A decision on one lawyer's effort to delay the start of next week's parliamentary session in Quebec — until MNAs take the Oath of Allegiance — will be made today.

Lawrence David, a constitutional lawyer and University of Ottawa professor, is asking Quebec's Superior Court to delay the beginning of parliamentary work, claiming that until all MNAs take the oath to the King, any laws they pass will be illegitimate.
David has filed a lawsuit and an emergency injuction to suspend Bill 4, a provincial law passed in 2022 that made taking the oath optional for members of the National Assembly.
MNAs elected in October's general election took an oath to the people of Quebec — instead of to the monarchy — at swearing-in ceremonies last month.

items: Renouncing oath to the King threatens National Assembly's legitimacy, lawyer argues

blocks.text: During the election campaign earlier this year, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, Parti Québécois leader and current Quebec premier, said that his government would defund the office of Quebec's lieutenant-governor.
The premier further promised to "abolish whatever monarchy exists in Quebec."
Quebec Superior Court Justice Ian Demers is expected to deliver his decision on the injunction at a Montreal courthouse around 10 a.m.
The decision comes just over a week before the National Assembly is set to resume on Dec. 1.
The parliamentary session was initially supposed to begin on Nov. 17, before being pushed back twice — first to Nov. 24, then to the beginning of December.
